facts.fact: Article 52 creates the office of President; Article 53 vests the executive power of the Union in the President.
The President is elected by elected members of both Houses of Parliament and of the State Legislative Assemblies (Art 54).
Elected members of the Delhi and Puducherry Assemblies were added to the electoral college by the 70th Amendment, 1992.
Nominated MPs, nominated MLAs and members of Legislative Councils do not vote in the presidential election.
An MLA's vote value is the state's 1971-census population divided by its elected MLAs and by 1,000; MPs' votes keep parity with the states.
The President is elected by proportional representation by single transferable vote, by secret ballot (Art 55).
A presidential nomination needs at least 50 proposers and 50 seconders.
A presidential candidate deposits ₹15,000 in the Reserve Bank of India.
To be President one must be a citizen, have completed 35 years and be qualified for Lok Sabha membership (Art 58).
A sitting Vice-President, Governor or Union/State minister may contest for President; these are not offices of profit.
Disputes over the election of the President or Vice-President are decided only by the Supreme Court (Art 71).
The President takes oath before the Chief Justice of India (Art 60).
Under Article 59 the President gets a rent-free residence and emoluments that cannot be reduced during the term.
Under Article 361 no criminal proceedings lie against the President during the term; civil cases need two months' notice.
The President resigns by writing to the Vice-President.
The only ground for impeaching the President is violation of the Constitution (Art 61).
Impeachment charges need the signatures of one-fourth of the House and 14 days' notice.
An impeachment resolution must pass by two-thirds of the total membership of each House.
Nominated MPs take part in impeachment, though they do not vote in the election; elected MLAs do not take part.
No President of India has ever been impeached.
An election to fill a casual vacancy in the office of President must be held within six months (Art 62).
A President elected to a vacancy serves a full five-year term.
If both President and Vice-President offices are vacant the CJI acts (1969 Act); M. Hidayatullah did so in 1969.
The President cannot return a Money Bill (no suspensive veto) but may assent or withhold.
The President must assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill (24th Amendment, 1971).
Absolute veto was used by Rajendra Prasad (1954, PEPSU Appropriation Bill) and R. Venkataraman (1991).
Zail Singh used the pocket veto on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill in 1986.
The Constitution sets no time limit for presidential assent, unlike the US 10-day limit, enabling the pocket veto.
A bill re-passed after a suspensive veto, even by simple majority, must receive assent.
Article 123 lets the President issue ordinances only when either House is not in session.
An ordinance lapses six weeks after Parliament reassembles; the maximum life is six months and six weeks.
An ordinance can be retrospective but cannot amend the Constitution.
R.C. Cooper (1970) allowed challenge to ordinance satisfaction; the 38th Amendment barred it and the 44th restored review.
Repeated re-promulgation of ordinances is a fraud on the Constitution (D.C. Wadhwa 1987; Krishna Kumar Singh 2017).
Art 72 pardon covers Union-law offences, court-martial sentences and death sentences.
A pardon removes both the sentence and the conviction.
Commutation substitutes a lighter form of punishment; remission shortens the period without changing its character.
Respite awards a lesser sentence for a special fact; reprieve stays the execution of a sentence.
Maru Ram (1980) held that the pardoning power is exercised on ministerial advice.
Kehar Singh (1989) held there is no right to an oral hearing in a mercy petition.
Epuru Sudhakar (2006), an Andhra Pradesh case, held arbitrary pardons subject to judicial review.
Unlike the President, a Governor cannot pardon a court-martial sentence or pardon a death sentence (Art 161).
The President appoints the AG, CAG, CEC, UPSC members, Governors and the Finance Commission.
The President nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha.
The President has situational discretion in a hung House or when a PM dies without a successor.
The President may return ministerial advice once for reconsideration (44th Amendment); then must act on it.
Article 86 lets the President address either House or both Houses.
The President is the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces.
Rajendra Prasad, the first President, is the only one to serve two full terms.
Zakir Husain was the first Muslim President and the first to die in office (1969).
V.V. Giri served both as Acting President and as President.
Neelam Sanjiva Reddy, the first Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh, is the only President elected unopposed (1977).
K.R. Narayanan was the first Dalit President.
Pratibha Patil was the first woman President.
Droupadi Murmu is the 15th President, in office since 25 July 2022, the first tribal woman President.
Article 63 creates the Vice-President, who is ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Art 64).
The Vice-President is elected by all members of both Houses, elected and nominated, with no state MLAs (Art 66).
The 11th Amendment (1961) removed the requirement of a joint meeting of the Houses to elect the Vice-President.
A Vice-President must be 35 and qualified for Rajya Sabha membership.
A vice-presidential nomination needs 20 proposers and 20 seconders and a ₹15,000 deposit.
The Vice-President takes oath before the President (Art 69).
The Vice-President resigns to the President.
Removal of the Vice-President starts only in the Rajya Sabha by effective majority with 14 days' notice, agreed by the Lok Sabha by simple majority.
No ground is stated in the Constitution for removing the Vice-President.
When acting as President (up to six months) the Vice-President does not chair the Rajya Sabha and draws the President's salary.
The Vice-President is paid as Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, not as Vice-President.
India's Vice-President is modelled on the American one, but only acts as President and does not succeed to the term.
Article 70 lets Parliament provide for discharge of the President's functions in other contingencies.
S. Radhakrishnan was the first Vice-President of India.
Jagdeep Dhankhar resigned as Vice-President on 21 July 2025 on health grounds.
C.P. Radhakrishnan became the 15th Vice-President on 12 September 2025, defeating B. Sudershan Reddy.
The PM is appointed by the President under Article 75; no procedure is laid down.
Presidential discretion in appointing a PM was first used in 1979 (Charan Singh).
The PM may belong to either House; Rajya Sabha PMs include Indira Gandhi, Deve Gowda, Gujral and Manmohan Singh.
Article 78 makes it the PM's duty to communicate Cabinet decisions to the President.
The PM chairs NITI Aayog, the Inter-State Council, the National Integration Council and the National Water Resources Council.
Narendra Modi was sworn in for a third consecutive term on 9 June 2024.
The PM's death or resignation dissolves the whole Council of Ministers.
The 42nd Amendment (1976) made ministerial advice binding on the President.
Under Article 74(2) no court may inquire into the advice given by ministers to the President.
Total ministers including the PM may not exceed 15% of the Lok Sabha (Art 75(1A), 91st Amendment 2003).
A member disqualified for defection cannot be appointed minister (Art 75(1B), 91st Amendment).
The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Art 75(3)).
A non-member minister must enter Parliament within six months (Art 75(5)).
India has no legal responsibility of ministers; orders of the President need no ministerial countersignature.
Under Article 77 all executive action is taken in the name of the President.
Under Article 88 ministers and the AG may speak in either House or a committee but vote only where they are members.
The Council has three tiers: Cabinet ministers, Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers; Parliamentary Secretaries are outside it.
The word Cabinet appears only in Article 352, inserted by the 44th Amendment (1978).
A Kitchen Cabinet is the PM's informal inner circle, powerful under Indira Gandhi.
Cabinet committees are extra-constitutional; Political Affairs is the super cabinet, and Parliamentary Affairs advises on summoning.
The Attorney General (Art 76) must be qualified to be a Supreme Court judge and is appointed by the President.
The AG holds office during the pleasure of the President with no fixed term.
The AG has the right of audience in all courts of India.
The AG is not a member of the Cabinet and may take private practice.
M.C. Setalvad was the first Attorney General; R. Venkataramani holds the post now.
The Solicitor General (Tushar Mehta) is a statutory, not constitutional, officer.
Parliament consists of the President, the Rajya Sabha and the Lok Sabha (Art 79); Articles 79-122 are in Part V.
Indian Parliament is modelled on the British Westminster system.
Rajya Sabha maximum is 250 (238 elected + 12 nominated); its present strength is 245.
The 12 nominated Rajya Sabha members have special knowledge of literature, science, art and social service (Art 80(3)).
Rajya Sabha seats are allotted by population in the Fourth Schedule; Uttar Pradesh has the most (31).
Only Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu & Kashmir among UTs have Rajya Sabha seats.
Rajya Sabha members are elected by MLAs by STV with an open ballot since 2003.
The domicile requirement for Rajya Sabha was removed in 2003, upheld in Kuldip Nayar (2006).
Rajya Sabha is a permanent House; members serve six years and one-third retire every two years.
The Lok Sabha has 543 elected members; maximum 530 from states and 20 from UTs.
The 104th Amendment (2019) ended nomination of two Anglo-Indians to the Lok Sabha.
Andhra Pradesh has 25 Lok Sabha and 11 Rajya Sabha seats.
Lok Sabha seat allocation is frozen on the 1971 census till the first census after 2026 (42nd and 84th Amendments).
Constituency boundaries were readjusted on the 2001 census by the 87th Amendment (2003).
Article 330 reserves Lok Sabha seats for SCs and STs.
The 106th Amendment (2023), Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, reserves one-third of seats for women (Art 330A) for 15 years after delimitation.
The Lok Sabha term is five years (Art 83); in a National Emergency it can be extended a year at a time, up to six months after the emergency.
Article 84: a member must be a citizen, take oath before an ECI-authorised person, and be 30 (RS) or 25 (LS).
The RPA 1951 requires a candidate to be a registered elector.
Article 102 disqualifies for office of profit, unsound mind, undischarged insolvency or non-citizenship.
Under the RPA a conviction with imprisonment of two years or more disqualifies a member.
Lily Thomas (2013) struck down Section 8(4) of the RPA.
Under Article 103 the President decides Art 102 disqualification on the binding opinion of the Election Commission.
The Tenth Schedule came by the 52nd Amendment (1985).
Defection grounds: voluntarily giving up membership, defying the whip, an independent joining a party.
A nominated member is disqualified only if he joins a party after six months.
A merger backed by two-thirds of the legislature party is exempt; the 91st Amendment deleted the one-third split exception.
Kihoto Hollohan (1992) made the Speaker's defection decision subject to judicial review.
Keisham Meghachandra (2020) asked Speakers to decide defection petitions within about three months.
A seat falls vacant for double membership or absence for 60 days without permission (Art 101).
Article 105 gives freedom of speech in the House and immunity for votes and speeches.
Members are free from arrest in civil cases 40 days before and after a session.
Sita Soren (2024) held no immunity for bribery, overruling P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998).
Article 100 fixes the quorum at one-tenth of the House.
Under Article 120 business is in Hindi or English.
Article 121 bars discussion of a judge's conduct except on a removal motion.
Article 122 bars courts from inquiring into proceedings of Parliament.
Article 118 lets each House make its rules of procedure.
An ordinary bill may start in either House and does not lapse on prorogation (Art 107).
Article 109: a Money Bill starts only in the Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation; the Rajya Sabha has 14 days.
A Money Bill (Art 110) deals only with taxes, borrowing, the Consolidated or Contingency Fund, appropriation and charged expenditure.
A bill is not a Money Bill merely because it provides for fines, licence fees or local-authority taxes.
Financial Bills (Art 117): 117(1) bills start only in the Lok Sabha; 117(3) bills may start in either House.
The Speaker's certificate that a bill is a Money Bill is final (Art 110(3)).
K.S. Puttaswamy (2018) upheld the Aadhaar Act as a Money Bill; Rojer Mathew (2019) referred the issue to a larger bench.
The Speaker resigns to the Deputy Speaker.
The Speaker is removed by an effective majority of the Lok Sabha after 14 days' notice.
During a removal resolution the Speaker cannot preside but may speak and vote in the first instance, without a casting vote.
The Speaker does not vacate office on dissolution and continues until the new House first meets.
The Speaker does not vote in the first instance but has a casting vote in a tie.
The Speaker certifies Money Bills and decides Tenth Schedule disqualification.
Om Birla (Kota) was re-elected Speaker on 26 June 2024 by voice vote; a removal motion was defeated on 11 March 2026.
G.V. Mavalankar was the first Speaker; M. Ananthasayanam Ayyangar the first Deputy Speaker.
The Speaker's salary is charged on the Consolidated Fund and the Speaker ranks with the CJI in precedence.
The Speaker chairs the Business Advisory, Rules and General Purposes Committees.
The Deputy Speaker's post has been vacant since 2019.
The Deputy Speaker is elected by the Lok Sabha under Article 93 and resigns to the Speaker.
The Speaker pro tem is appointed by the President, usually the senior-most member; Bhartruhari Mahtab in 2024.
The Speaker nominates a Panel of Chairpersons of up to 10, who cannot preside when both Speaker and Deputy posts are vacant.
The Rajya Sabha Chairman does not certify Money Bills or preside at joint sittings.
Harivansh Narayan Singh is Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (since 2018).
The Leader of the Opposition leads the largest opposition party with one-tenth of the seats; statutory since 1977.
Rahul Gandhi is Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha and Mallikarjun Kharge in the Rajya Sabha.
J.P. Nadda is Leader of the House in the Rajya Sabha; the PM leads the Lok Sabha.
The whip rests only on convention; it is not in the Constitution, the Rules or a statute.
Article 85: the gap between sessions cannot exceed six months.
The President summons Parliament on the advice of the Cabinet Committee on Parliamentary Affairs.
The three sessions (Budget, Monsoon, Winter) are a convention; the Constitution fixes no number or minimum days.
A day's sittings run 11 am-1 pm and 2-6 pm.
Adjournment sine die is ordered by the presiding officer; prorogation by the President.
A bill pending in the Lok Sabha, or passed by it and pending in the Rajya Sabha, lapses on dissolution.
Bills in the Rajya Sabha not passed by the Lok Sabha, bills notified for a joint sitting, awaiting assent or returned do not lapse.
Quorum is 55 in the Lok Sabha and 25 in the Rajya Sabha.
A lame-duck session is the last session of the outgoing Lok Sabha.
The Official Languages Act 1963 allowed English to continue after 1965.
A joint sitting (Art 108) passes a bill by a majority of members present and voting.
Joint sittings were held only for Dowry Prohibition (1961), Banking Service Commission Repeal (1978) and POTA (2002).
A joint sitting is presided over by the Speaker, then the Deputy Speaker, then the Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman.
Money Bills and Constitutional Amendment Bills cannot go to a joint sitting.
The new Parliament building was inaugurated on 28 May 2023.
Starred questions get oral answers with supplementaries; unstarred get written answers.
A short-notice question is asked with less than 10 days' notice and answered orally.
Zero Hour is an Indian innovation since 1962, not in the rules.
An adjournment motion is admitted only in the Lok Sabha with 50 members, involves censure and lasts at least 2½ hours.
The calling attention motion is an Indian innovation of 1954 and is in the rules.
A no-confidence motion (Rule 198) needs 50 members and no reasons; the first was by J.B. Kripalani against Nehru in 1963.
A censure motion must state reasons, may target a minister and need not force resignation.
A short-duration discussion is under Rule 193 for two hours, with no formal motion.
Rule 377 in the Lok Sabha corresponds to Special Mention in the Rajya Sabha.
Kangaroo closure debates only important clauses; guillotine closure puts undiscussed clauses to vote.
Defeat of the Motion of Thanks on the President's address means defeat of the government.
Confidence votes were lost by V.P. Singh (1990), Deve Gowda (1997) and Vajpayee (1999, by one vote).
Private members' resolutions are discussed on alternate Fridays.
Parliament controls the Council of Ministers through adjournment motions, Question Hour and supplementary questions (UPSC 2017).
The PAC (1921) has 22 members (15 LS + 7 RS) and examines CAG reports.
The PAC chair has come from the Opposition since 1967 and ministers cannot be members.
The Estimates Committee (1950, John Mathai) has 30 Lok Sabha members and is the largest.
The Committee on Public Undertakings (1964, Krishna Menon Committee) has 22 members.
There are 24 DRSCs (since 2004; first 1993) of 31 members — 16 under the Lok Sabha and 8 under the Rajya Sabha.
The Committee on Petitions has 15 Lok Sabha and 10 Rajya Sabha members.
Ethics Committees were set up in the Rajya Sabha (1997) and the Lok Sabha (2000).
The Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs (1968) has 30 members (20 LS + 10 RS).
The Joint Committee on Offices of Profit has 15 members (10 LS + 5 RS).
JPCs are ad hoc committees of both Houses, e.g. Bofors (1987) and the Harshad Mehta scam (1992).
Consultative Committees are run by the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs and are not parliamentary committees.
The budget is the Annual Financial Statement (Art 112); the word budget is not used in the Constitution.
Charged expenditure is not votable but discussable; demands need the President's recommendation (Art 113).
No amendment varying the amount can be moved to the Appropriation Bill (Art 114).
Article 115 covers supplementary, additional and excess grants.
Article 116 covers vote on account, vote of credit and exceptional grants.
No tax may be levied except by authority of law (Art 265).
Article 266 creates the Consolidated Fund and the Public Account.
The Contingency Fund (Art 267) is at the President's disposal, held by the Finance Secretary, corpus ₹30,000 crore.
High Court judges' pensions, CAG, UPSC expenses and debt charges are charged on the Consolidated Fund.
An excess grant is voted only after the PAC approves it.
An additional grant is for a new service not in the budget; a token grant pays for a new service by re-appropriation.
Under the Provisional Collection of Taxes Act 1931 the Finance Bill must be enacted within 75 days.
A vote on account is usually for two months and about one-sixth of the budget.
The budget is presented on 1 February since 2017, when the Railway Budget was merged.
The Railway Budget was separated in 1924 on the Acworth Committee's advice.
R.K. Shanmukham Chetty presented independent India's first budget on 26 November 1947.
Nirmala Sitharaman presented the 2026-27 budget in February 2026, her ninth consecutive.
Policy cut reduces a demand to Re 1, economy cut by a stated amount, token cut by ₹100.
Only the Lok Sabha votes on Demands for Grants.
MPLADS was launched on 23 December 1993 and run by MoSPI since October 1994.
Each MP gets ₹5 crore a year under MPLADS; it was suspended in 2020-22 for COVID-19.
MPLADS earmarks at least 15% for SC and 7.5% for ST areas.
Nominated MPs may choose MPLADS works anywhere in India; elected Rajya Sabha MPs anywhere in their state.
MPLADS funds are non-lapsable, released to the district authority, which inspects at least 10% of works.
The Department of Personnel was created in 1970 under the PM, after the N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar Committee and the ARC (1966).
